Producing standard capacity forecasts and resource budgets independently is Dreyfus's advanced-beginner band: applying familiar demand-forecasting methods from the SRE book's capacity-planning chapter to known workloads.

Planning capacity autonomously and modeling demand/headroom/resource trade-offs is the Dreyfus competent band: the SRE book's organic-plus-inorganic-growth forecasting model, applied to ambiguous demand-shift cases, is exactly this level's ownership judgment.

Defining capacity-planning approaches teams adopt and solving hard forecasting/efficiency problems is Dreyfus's proficient stage and SFIA level 5 (Ensure, advise): the practitioner's forecasting method, grounded in the SRE book's capacity-planning chapter, becomes what other teams are advised to reuse.

Setting capacity and resource-budgeting strategy across systems and anticipating long-term demand shifts is SFIA level 6 (Initiate, influence): org-wide budgeting direction across many systems' headroom, per the SRE book's capacity-strategy practice, not one service's forecast.

The Google SRE book's capacity-planning chapter defined the reference forecasting and budgeting practice the industry now builds on, matching the discipline-defining SFIA level 7 (Set strategy, inspire, mobilise) / Dreyfus mastery band.

Mapping and documenting existing process steps under guidance, flagging obvious bottlenecks for review, is the novice band: following a defined mapping method without discretion over what to redesign.
Independently running standard process improvements -- identifying waste per Womack & Jones's value-stream mapping and implementing routine fixes with normal review -- is the advanced-beginner band.

Autonomously redesigning ambiguous, cross-team processes end-to-end is the competent band -- Hammer & Champy's reengineering explicitly requires starting from a blank page rather than optimizing an existing flow, which is judgment with no fixed method to follow.

Defining the improvement methodology other teams adopt and untangling processes others find intractable is SFIA's ensure/advise level -- the practitioner's redesign approach becomes the org's standard reengineering method.

Setting operational-excellence strategy across the business and anticipating where process capability must head next is SFIA's initiate/influence level -- enterprise-wide scope beyond any one process.

Operational practice recognized industry-wide and sought externally -- the standing lean thinking achieved as a cross-industry management discipline beyond its Toyota origin -- is SFIA's top set-strategy level.
Documenting current roles, handoffs, and reporting lines under direction for a single team is the novice band: recording a given structure without discretion over design choices.

Independently designing structure for one function, clarifying routine roles and decision rights with review, is the advanced-beginner band -- applying Galbraith's Star Model dimensions to a bounded, single-function redesign.

Autonomously designing operating models for ambiguous multi-function areas, resolving overlap and accountability gaps, is the competent band -- Nadler & Tushman's architecture-design judgment across units has no template, unlike single-function structuring.

Defining org-design approaches other designers follow and solving structural problems that have stumped leadership is SFIA's ensure/advise level -- the practitioner's application of the Star Model becomes the org's design method.
Setting enterprise operating-model strategy and anticipating structural shifts the organization will need is SFIA's initiate/influence level -- enterprise-wide design authority, not one function.

Shaping how the discipline conceives operating models, externally recognized for the craft, is SFIA's top set-strategy level -- the standing organizational-architecture scholarship achieves as a field reference.
Coordinating tasks and tracking actions for a small initiative under a lead's guidance is the novice band: executing defined coordination tasks with no discretion over how the initiative is run.

Independently running a defined cross-team initiative, managing routine dependencies and stakeholders with review, is the advanced-beginner band -- applying PMBOK's standard performance domains to a bounded initiative.

Autonomously leading ambiguous, contentious initiatives spanning many functions to landed outcomes is the competent band -- Bossidy & Charan's execution discipline is precisely the judgment-under-resistance that a defined project plan doesn't supply.

Defining how complex initiatives are run and rescuing efforts others cannot move is SFIA's ensure/advise level -- the practitioner's execution approach becomes the org's method, beyond running any one initiative well.

Setting the strategy and operating cadence for the organization's most critical cross-functional bets is SFIA's initiate/influence level -- portfolio-wide authority over which initiatives matter and how they run.

Industry-leading practice for cross-functional execution, sought externally to teach it, is SFIA's top set-strategy level -- the standing a body of knowledge like PMBOK achieves as the field's shared standard.

Configuring simple GTM workflow and field changes under supervision, following established conventions, is the novice band: executing defined configuration tasks without discretion over system design.

Independently building and maintaining standard revenue workflows and integrations with normal review is the advanced-beginner band -- correctly implementing known building blocks of the revenue stack per Diorio & Hummel's systems model.

Autonomously designing end-to-end GTM system architecture across marketing, sales, and success, handling messy edge cases, is the competent band -- Diorio & Hummel's nine-building-block system requires connecting the whole stack, not implementing one workflow, which has no fixed template for a given org's edge cases.
Defining the revenue-systems blueprint others adopt and solving integration problems others can't is SFIA's ensure/advise level -- the practitioner's architecture becomes the org's RevOps standard.
Setting RevOps systems strategy and anticipating how the GTM tech stack must evolve is SFIA's initiate/influence level -- enterprise-wide authority over the whole revenue system, not one integration.

Defining what good revenue operations looks like for the field and being externally credible on it is SFIA's top set-strategy level -- the standing RevOps has achieved as a named discipline with its own literature and practitioner community.
Pulling standard pipeline and funnel reports under guidance, checking figures before sharing, is the novice band: executing a defined reporting task without discretion over which metrics matter.

Independently building routine revenue analyses and dashboards, explaining trends with normal review, is the advanced-beginner band -- correctly computing and reporting Skok's standard SaaS metrics (CAC, LTV, churn) rather than defining new ones.

Autonomously modeling ambiguous revenue questions end-to-end and becoming the trusted source for GTM numbers is the competent band -- deciding which of Skok's metric framework applies to a novel revenue question, and defending the model, has no fixed procedure.

Defining the analytical frameworks and metric definitions other revenue teams adopt is SFIA's ensure/advise level -- the practitioner's metric definitions become the org's standard, the same role Skok's own framework plays industry-wide.

Setting revenue-analytics strategy and anticipating which signals will drive future growth decisions is SFIA's initiate/influence level -- authority over the whole measurement system, not one dashboard.

Shaping how the discipline measures revenue performance, recognized externally for the methods, is SFIA's top set-strategy level -- the standing Skok's SaaS Metrics framework achieved as the field's reference vocabulary for revenue measurement.
Processing standard deal desk requests and applying approved discount rules under review is the novice band: executing given rules without discretion over pricing judgment.

Independently managing routine pricing approvals and deal structuring within set guardrails is the advanced-beginner band -- applying Nagle, Hogan & Zale's value-based pricing policy correctly to a standard deal, not setting the policy.

Autonomously structuring complex, non-standard deals and setting local norms for monetization mechanics is the competent band -- Nagle, Hogan & Zale's pricing-policy layer exists precisely because non-standard deals require judgment a price list can't encode.

Defining deal-desk and monetization approaches others follow and cracking pricing problems others can't is SFIA's ensure/advise level -- the practitioner's pricing policy becomes the org's method, beyond applying value-based pricing well.
Setting monetization and pricing-operations strategy and anticipating shifts in how value is captured is SFIA's initiate/influence level -- enterprise-wide pricing authority, not one deal.

Leading practice for pricing operations across the field, sought externally for it, is SFIA's top set-strategy level -- the standing Nagle's value-based pricing framework achieved across decades of editions as the discipline's core text.
Updating forecast inputs and assembling planning templates under guidance is the novice band: populating a given template without discretion over forecasting method.

Independently producing standard forecasts and plans, reconciling routine variances with review, is the advanced-beginner band -- running a defined forecast cycle correctly, not yet questioning whether the cycle itself fits the business.

Autonomously building forecasting models for ambiguous situations and owning the planning cadence end-to-end is the competent band -- Hope & Fraser's central claim is that rigid annual budgeting fails precisely where judgment must replace the fixed cycle, which is the P2-to-P3 boundary.

Defining the forecasting methodology others adopt and resolving planning problems others cannot is SFIA's ensure/advise level -- the practitioner's adaptive planning approach becomes the org's method, echoing Hope & Fraser's beyond-budgeting model being adopted org-wide.
Setting enterprise planning strategy and anticipating the dynamics future forecasts must capture is SFIA's initiate/influence level -- authority over the whole planning system, not one cycle.

Best-in-class forecasting practice recognized externally is SFIA's top set-strategy level -- the standing the Beyond Budgeting Round Table achieved as a cross-industry reference model for planning practice.
Building basic reports and dashboards from defined requirements under supervision is the novice band: executing a given spec without discretion over what to measure.

Independently delivering standard BI analyses and self-serve dashboards with normal review is the advanced-beginner band -- correctly building on Kimball's dimensional-modeling conventions rather than defining new semantic structures.

Autonomously framing ambiguous business questions and building the analytics the organization relies on is the competent band -- Davenport & Harris's stage model shows this is where an org moves past reporting into analytics that actually answers undefined questions, requiring judgment no dashboard spec supplies.

Defining BI standards, semantic models, and methods others adopt across the business is SFIA's ensure/advise level -- the practitioner's schema and metric definitions become the org's standard, the role Kimball's dimensional-modeling method plays industry-wide.

Setting the operational-analytics strategy and anticipating the decisions data must soon support is SFIA's initiate/influence level -- Davenport & Harris's higher maturity stages describe exactly this org-wide anticipatory analytics posture.

Shaping how the discipline practices business intelligence, externally credible on it, is SFIA's top set-strategy level -- the standing Davenport & Harris's analytical-competitor model achieved as the field's reference framework.
Performing defined data cleanup and quality checks under guidance, escalating anomalies, is the novice band: executing given quality rules without discretion over what quality requires here.

Independently maintaining data standards and resolving routine quality issues with review is the advanced-beginner band -- applying Redman's quality dimensions (accuracy, completeness, timeliness) to known issue types.

Autonomously designing governance and quality controls for ambiguous, messy data domains is the competent band -- DAMA-DMBOK's stewardship function requires designing controls for domains with no established rulebook, unlike applying Redman's known dimensions to a defined issue.

Defining the governance framework others adopt and remediating data problems others can't is SFIA's ensure/advise level -- the practitioner's stewardship model becomes the org's DAMA-DMBOK-aligned standard.
Setting enterprise data-governance strategy and anticipating emerging quality and stewardship needs is SFIA's initiate/influence level -- authority over the whole governance program, not one domain.

What good operational data governance means for the field, externally recognized, is SFIA's top set-strategy level -- the standing DAMA-DMBOK itself achieved as the discipline's body-of-knowledge reference.
Performing routine system configuration and user support tasks under supervision is the novice band: executing defined configuration steps without discretion over system design.

Independently administering business systems and building standard workflows with normal review is the advanced-beginner band -- correctly following ITIL 4's service-request and change-enablement practices for known request types.

Autonomously designing complex automations and system configurations, handling tricky edge cases, is the competent band -- ITIL 4's value-stream design requires judgment for cases the standard practices don't script, unlike routine service requests.

Defining administration standards and architecture others adopt and fixing what others cannot is SFIA's ensure/advise level -- the practitioner's system design becomes the org's operating standard, beyond running ITIL practices well.
Setting business-systems strategy and anticipating how the workflow platform landscape must evolve is SFIA's initiate/influence level -- enterprise-wide platform authority, not one system.

Leading practice for business-systems administration, sought externally for it, is SFIA's top set-strategy level -- the standing ITSM frameworks like ITIL achieve as the field's shared standard, adopted and taught worldwide.
Communicating status clearly with accurate documentation is the novice band -- Zinsser's baseline clarity discipline: say what happened, plainly.

Writing clear design notes, runbooks and PRs, and explaining trade-offs without overselling, is the advanced-beginner band -- Zinsser's 'clutter is the disease' discipline applied to routine technical writing.

Writing design docs that drive decisions and translating technical risk for non-technical stakeholders is the competent band and requires Minto's answer-first, pyramid-structured argument -- leading with the conclusion a decision-maker needs.

Making complex capability/risk legible to executives without dumbing it down, and having RFCs align orgs, is Minto's pyramid principle applied at the scale of documents that must persuade rooms full of stakeholders at once.
Strategy memos leadership acts on, with org-wide and external reach, is SFIA9's strategic-influence band -- writing that changes org direction, not just informs it.

Being a clarifying voice at company scale, externally recognized, is Dreyfus's master band -- the level Zinsser's decades of teaching writers aimed to reach: clarity that carries beyond one's own organization.
Sharing what they learn and keeping their docs accurate is the novice band -- Stepper's first Working Out Loud habit of simply making one's work visible.
Documenting their area well and proactively sharing techniques with the team is the advanced-beginner band -- Stepper's narrating-work practice extended into a habit, not a one-off post.

Creating documentation and forums that raise a whole domain's understanding is the competent band -- Stepper's relationship-building through visible work scaled to a domain of people, not just individual narration.

Building knowledge-sharing systems adopted across teams moves from personal practice to institutional infrastructure -- the kind of documented, org-wide practice published career ladders like GitLab's expect at senior engineering levels.
Defining how the org captures and spreads knowledge is SFIA9's strategic-influence band -- designing the knowledge system, not populating it.
Shaping industry-facing knowledge practice is Dreyfus's master band -- the level at which a practice like Working Out Loud becomes an externally adopted movement rather than one person's habit.
Being responsive to feedback, pairing willingly, and asking for help appropriately is the novice band -- the trust-building forming stage of Tuckman's model, taken individually.
Collaborating smoothly with adjacent functions and handling disagreement constructively is the advanced-beginner band -- navigating Tuckman's storming stage without derailing the team.

Building strong cross-team relationships and resolving friction directly is the competent band and is Lencioni's trust-and-conflict foundation applied across team boundaries -- the first two dysfunctions actively countered, not just avoided.

Aligning teams with competing priorities and mediating disputes between senior people is Lencioni's dysfunction model applied where accountability and results are contested between teams, not individuals -- resolving the harder, structural dysfunctions.

Creating the forums and processes through which collaboration happens is SFIA9's strategic-influence band combined with Team Topologies' case for deliberately designing team interaction modes rather than letting them emerge.
Building coalitions at company scale and externally is Dreyfus's master band -- sustained, healthy team function beyond any one team, the outcome Lencioni's model is built to produce at scale.
Accepting feedback non-defensively and acting on it is the novice band -- the receiving-feedback skill Stone & Heen treat as foundational and non-trivial, not something people arrive already good at.
Giving timely, specific, kind feedback to peers is the advanced-beginner band -- Scott's 'care personally, challenge directly' quadrant applied to routine peer feedback.

Giving growth-oriented feedback that changes behavior, coaching through feedback, is the competent band and is Radical Candor's harder discipline -- challenging directly enough that behavior actually changes, not just noting the issue.
Building feedback norms that raise the bar across teams is Radical Candor applied as an instituted team practice rather than one person's individual habit -- norms others are held to.

Setting the org's culture of candor and growth is SFIA9's strategic-influence band -- Scott's own argument that radical candor has to be modeled and built into culture from leadership down, not left to individual managers.
Modeling and defining feedback culture company-wide is Dreyfus's master band -- the level at which a leader's feedback practice becomes the company's, the aim Scott's book sets for its readers.
Voicing disagreement respectfully and disagreeing-and-committing is the novice band -- Fisher & Ury's baseline of separating people from the problem, practiced individually.
Working through disagreement to a decision without damaging relationships is the advanced-beginner band -- applying principled-negotiation moves to reach a decision, not just state a position.

Mediating technical disputes in their domain and finding the path that holds up is the competent band and is what Crucial Conversations calls stepping into dialogue when stakes, opinions, and emotions are all high -- mediating, not just negotiating one's own position.
Resolving high-stakes disagreements between senior stakeholders across orgs is Crucial Conversations' toolkit applied where the stakes and organizational distance are both highest.

Designing the decision processes the org uses to resolve conflict is SFIA9's strategic-influence band -- building the structure for disagreement to resolve well, not resolving each instance personally.

Setting the company norm for principled disagreement is Dreyfus's master band -- the level at which Fisher & Ury's 'insist on objective criteria' becomes how a whole company disagrees, not one negotiator's technique.

Preparing status updates for leadership with guidance, leading with the headline when coached to, is the novice band -- following Minto's answer-first structure because someone reminds them to, not yet by habit.
Reporting upward answer-first with a specific ask, escalating early with options attached, is the advanced-beginner band -- Minto's pyramid principle applied as a self-sufficient habit.

Briefing senior leaders under pressure with facts, impact, options, and a recommendation inside two minutes is the competent band and is Grove's case for a manager's output being measured in the output of the organizations under their influence -- communication precise enough to drive that output without wasting a leader's attention.

Building and landing investment cases with executive audiences, pre-wired with skeptics and sized in business terms, is Minto's pyramid principle deployed at the scale of a decision that must survive hostile scrutiny, plus coaching others to do the same.

Operating the executive room as a peer, absorbing hostile questioning and changing the room's decision, is SFIA9's highest strategic-influence band combined with Grove's account of the high-leverage activities -- like decisions made in meetings among peers -- that define senior management work.

Speaking for an organization's technical reality to boards, investors, and press, with organizational credibility on the line, is Dreyfus's master band -- Grove's output-of-a-manager principle extended to speaking for the organization's credibility itself.

Logging and triaging tickets by set scripts, escalating anything beyond well-defined fixes, is ITIL 4's incident/request-management practice run with no situational judgment — the Dreyfus novice band.
Resolving standard incidents and requests independently within SLA is the same ITIL 4 practices run competently on routine variation without escalation — the Dreyfus advanced-beginner band.

Owning ambiguous, high-impact incidents end-to-end and setting local triage conventions is HDI's Team Lead tier — coordinating escalation and setting process for a team, not just following it — the Dreyfus competent band.

Designing the ticket taxonomy, SLA tiers, and routing model other support staff adopt is HDI's Support Center Manager tier applied to process design, matching SFIA's ensure/advise responsibility level.

Setting service-management strategy and metrics across the whole support function is SFIA's initiate/influence responsibility band, turning ITIL 4's continual-improvement practice into enforced organizational policy rather than one team's convention.

Defining what good service management looks like for the discipline and shaping external practice is the ITIL Master tier's own bar — proposing and defending original service-management approaches to a review panel — the Dreyfus master band.

Preparing change records and gathering approvals for pre-templated, low-risk changes under review is ITIL 4's change-enablement practice run as scripted paperwork, not judgment — the Dreyfus novice band.

Planning and executing standard changes independently, with usable rollback steps and impact notes, is the same change-enablement practice run competently on routine work — the Dreyfus advanced-beginner band.

Owning risky, multi-team changes and judging risk under ambiguity is exactly the change-authorization judgment ITIL 4 reserves for cases the standard workflow doesn't script — the Dreyfus competent band, the go-to coordinator.

Designing the change-control, risk-tiering, and CAB model others follow is applying the DevOps Handbook's Second Way — reducing approval friction while containing risk — as team-wide process design, SFIA's ensure/advise reach.

Setting release-governance strategy that balances velocity and stability is applying Accelerate's empirically validated finding that change failure rate and deployment frequency move together, not in tension, for elite performers — as enforced organizational policy.

Defining industry-credible release-management practice and shaping how the discipline operates is producing the kind of empirically grounded, externally adopted practice Accelerate's own research program represents — the Dreyfus master band.

Handling common how-to questions at the desk and escalating unfamiliar issues is explicit, rule-following practice — the Dreyfus novice band; HDI's entry Support Center Analyst tier covers exactly this scope.

Resolving most end-user problems independently and producing clear self-help guidance is HDI's Analyst tier performed competently and without escalation on routine issues — the Dreyfus advanced-beginner band.
Tackling the hardest user-enablement cases and setting local standards for guidance and onboarding is HDI's Team Lead tier — setting team practice, not just executing it — the Dreyfus competent band.

Designing the enablement program, training curriculum, and support model others deliver against is building training to Kirkpatrick's reaction/learning/behavior/results structure at program-design scope, SFIA's ensure/advise reach.

Setting organization-wide strategy for adoption, digital literacy, and support experience is applying Kirkpatrick's evaluation levels — especially level 4, organizational results — as the frame for a strategy spanning every team's enablement, not one program's curriculum.

Defining best-practice end-user enablement for the field and shaping how others teach it is externally credible contribution to training-evaluation practice itself, beyond applying Kirkpatrick's model — the Dreyfus master band.

Enrolling, imaging, and configuring devices from documented build steps under supervision is NIST SP 800-124's mobile-device enrollment baseline followed by checklist, not judgment — the Dreyfus novice band.

Managing device fleets, policies, and patching independently for standard configurations is running SP 800-124's device-management baseline competently across routine variation without escalation — the Dreyfus advanced-beginner band.

Resolving complex endpoint, compliance, and policy issues and setting local device-management standards is applying CIS Controls v8's Safeguards (inventory, secure configuration) to cases the baseline checklist doesn't resolve — the Dreyfus competent band.

Designing the endpoint architecture, policy baseline, and lifecycle model others implement is authoring an organization's own Control 1/Control 4 implementation others follow, SFIA's ensure/advise reach.

Setting endpoint strategy across platforms, anticipating shifts in management and security posture, is SFIA's initiate/influence band applied to migrating endpoint trust from perimeter assumptions toward the device-posture checks NIST SP 800-207's zero-trust architecture requires.

Defining authoritative endpoint-management practice and influencing the discipline externally is the expert-consensus contribution that builds CIS Controls itself — a global practitioner community authoring the standard, not just applying it — the Dreyfus master band.

Configuring user accounts, groups, and shared spaces by set procedure is the entry associate-level scope Microsoft's Administrator Expert path presupposes before independent work — the Dreyfus novice band.

Administering collaboration services independently — routine config, permissions, issues — is exactly the associate-certification (Endpoint/Teams/Identity Administrator) scope performed competently without escalation — the Dreyfus advanced-beginner band.

Resolving complex platform, governance, and integration problems and setting local configuration standards is the tenant-wide judgment the MS-102 Administrator Expert exam tests — identity, security, and compliance governance across the estate — the Dreyfus competent band.

Designing the platform architecture, governance, and adoption model administrators follow moves from passing the Expert exam's scenarios to authoring the tenant governance model those scenarios assume, SFIA's ensure/advise reach.

Setting collaboration-platform strategy and roadmap across the whole workplace estate is SFIA's initiate/influence responsibility band, applied beyond one tenant's governance model to organizational technology strategy.

Defining leading collaboration-platform practice and shaping how the discipline is run elsewhere is externally credible, discipline-shaping contribution beyond any one organization's tenant — the Dreyfus master band.
Performing routine application config and user-provisioning tasks under guidance is ITIL 4's service-request-management practice run by checklist — the Dreyfus novice band.
Administering an application independently — standard config and support tasks — is the same practice run competently on routine work without escalation — the Dreyfus advanced-beginner band.
Resolving complex configuration, upgrade, and data issues as the go-to admin is exercising the judgment ITIL 4 reserves for cases the standard runbook doesn't cover — the Dreyfus competent band.

Setting administration strategy and standards across the whole application portfolio is COBIT 2019's governance layer — aligning IT-enabled services with enterprise goals — applied at SFIA's initiate/influence band rather than one system's configuration.

Defining authoritative enterprise-application administration practice recognized beyond the organization is externally credible contribution to the governance discipline COBIT itself codifies — the Dreyfus master band.
Building simple, pre-specified integrations from templates under review is applying a single pattern from Hohpe & Woolf's catalog without yet choosing which pattern fits — the Dreyfus novice band.

Developing standard integrations and automated workflows independently is selecting and applying Enterprise Integration Patterns competently on routine, well-understood system pairs — the Dreyfus advanced-beginner band.

Designing complex, multi-system integrations and resolving the hardest data and reliability problems is composing Hohpe & Woolf's patterns to solve cases the catalog doesn't hand you pre-assembled — the Dreyfus competent band.

Defining the integration patterns, automation framework, and standards other builders adopt is publishing a house dialect of Enterprise Integration Patterns as team practice, SFIA's ensure/advise reach.

Setting integration and automation strategy across all business systems is SFIA's initiate/influence band, applied to which pattern language and platform the whole organization standardizes on rather than one integration.
Defining best-practice systems integration and influencing the broader discipline is externally credible pattern-catalog-shaping work in Hohpe & Woolf's own tradition — the Dreyfus master band.

Provisioning accounts and applying access requests through a defined approval workflow under review is NIST SP 800-53's AC-2 account-management control executed by checklist — the Dreyfus novice band.

Managing identities, groups, and access independently for standard joiner-mover-leaver flows is the same AC-2 practice run competently without escalation on routine changes — the Dreyfus advanced-beginner band.
Resolving complex access, entitlement, and recertification issues is exercising AC-6 least-privilege judgment on ambiguous cases the standard workflow doesn't resolve — the Dreyfus competent band.

Solving well-defined problems using known algorithms under review is the novice band: applying a named algorithm to a recognized problem shape.

Asking good questions to turn a vague task into a clear one is the novice band -- the Cynefin move of first recognizing you're not in the simple domain, then asking for help mapping it.
Independently turning a vague request into a workable plan is the advanced-beginner band, self-sufficient in Cynefin's complicated domain -- knowable with analysis -- but not yet the complex domain.

Thriving in ambiguity, framing the problem for others, and committing to an approach is the competent band and is exactly Cynefin's complex-domain leadership move -- probe-sense-respond because cause and effect are only clear in hindsight.
Creating clarity for multiple teams out of open-ended situations extends Cynefin's complex-domain framing across several teams' worth of ambiguity at once, not just one's own.

Defining direction where none exists at org scale is SFIA9's strategic-influence band -- the leader Snowden and Boone describe operating routinely in the chaotic domain and acting first to establish order.
Comfortable with the highest-uncertainty company bets is Dreyfus's master band -- sustained operation in Cynefin's chaotic quadrant where no framework yet applies.
Learning to estimate, surfacing blockers, and planning own tasks with guidance is the novice band -- following an estimation technique under someone else's check.
Estimating scoped work realistically and planning own 1-3 week projects is the advanced-beginner band, applying Cohn's relative-sizing and velocity techniques independently within a known scope.

Planning quarter-scale, multi-workstream efforts including dependencies is the competent band and requires Cohn's release-planning layer, not just iteration planning -- sequencing across workstreams with dependencies.

Expert-level planning of large programs that anticipates risk early is what PMBOK's performance domains formalize for program-scale planning -- planning where the work itself spans multiple teams' plans.
Planning org-level programs across quarters and years is SFIA9's strategic-influence band paired with PMBOK's standard for value-delivery planning at portfolio scale.
Shaping how the company plans major technical change is Dreyfus's master band -- setting the planning method itself, the level a body of knowledge like PMBOK codifies from industry practice.
Taking ownership of assigned tasks and being honest about progress and blockers is the novice band -- ownership scoped to one's own work, with visible reporting.

Owning components end-to-end and delivering committed work reliably is the advanced-beginner band, applying Willink & Babin's baseline of taking ownership of outcomes rather than excuses to a bounded component.

Owning a domain, landing multi-week efforts without surprises, and pushing back on unrealistic scope with reasons is the competent band -- Willink & Babin's ownership principle extended to a whole delivery domain, not a single task.

Owning cross-team initiatives, unblocking teams, and killing failing approaches early is ownership extended across teams the way Willink & Babin describe commanders owning outcomes beyond their own unit, and matches what DORA's research finds distinguishes high-performing delivery organizations.
Owning an org-level portfolio of bets and setting direction others follow is SFIA9's strategic-influence band -- accountability at the scale of a portfolio, not a program.
Being the go-to when something company-critical must land is Dreyfus's master band -- the level of trust Willink & Babin describe reserved for leaders proven under the highest stakes.
Understanding the capability they're building and who uses it is the novice band -- user awareness without yet making product decisions.

Framing own work in user/business outcomes, not just tasks, is the advanced-beginner band -- Cagan's baseline expectation that engineers understand the outcome their work serves, without yet owning discovery.

Treating their area as a product and using metrics to decide what to build for a domain is the competent band and is Torres's continuous-discovery habit of weekly customer contact driving build decisions -- not a one-time discovery phase.
Expert alignment of technical bets with product strategy across teams is Cagan's account of product leaders who connect strategy to multiple teams' roadmaps, beyond running one team's discovery.
Setting product direction for an org's technical surface is SFIA9's strategic-influence band combined with Perri's case for product strategy that ties vision to economic outcomes org-wide.
Shaping how the company creates value through technical products is Dreyfus's master band -- escaping the build trap at company scale, the transformation Perri's book is written to drive.

Stating what business outcome their current task serves, and treating infrastructure/license costs as real money, is the novice band -- cost-awareness at the level FinOps calls informing: seeing the numbers, not yet acting on them.

Checking whether shipped work actually moved its metric and weighing cost/maintenance burden in owned technical choices is the advanced-beginner band -- FinOps's optimizing phase applied to work one owns directly.

Framing a domain's technical decisions in cost-of-delay and revenue-risk terms, and redirecting effort when the numbers say the plan is wrong, is the competent band and is Reinertsen's economic-framework case for making cost of delay the single unit of measure for technical trade-offs.

Building the business case for cross-team technical investments with the largest return is Boehm's software-economics tradition of quantifying engineering investment in business terms applied at cross-team scale.

Aligning an org's technical strategy with its economics -- cost curves, velocity, risk -- is SFIA9's strategic-influence band paired with FinOps's operate-at-scale maturity, where cost accountability is owned organization-wide.

Advising company leadership on where technology changes the business model is Dreyfus's master band -- the level Perri argues separates feature factories from companies where product/technology strategy IS business strategy.

Running a scripted interview and logging notes under a senior researcher's guidance is Dreyfus's novice band and SFIA Level 2 Assist; Fitzpatrick's Mom Test names exactly this failure mode -- leading, biased questions -- as what a script and review catch before a researcher can trust their own judgment.

Planning and running discovery for one feature with normal review is Dreyfus's advanced-beginner band and SFIA Level 3 Apply; it matches Torres's baseline weekly customer-touchpoint habit -- a repeatable cadence run without redesigning the method each time.

Choosing which discovery method fits an ambiguous problem and separating signal from noise is Dreyfus's competent band; Cagan frames this method judgment against the four discovery risks (value, usability, feasibility, viability) as the skill separating a proficient PM from one following a fixed script.

Designing a discovery approach a whole team adopts and untangling contradictory findings is Dreyfus's proficient band, where practice becomes codified for reuse; this is the register Torres's opportunity-solution-tree method occupies -- a structure one person designs and a team runs against.

Setting research strategy across an organization and anticipating unstated needs before they surface is Dreyfus's expert band and SFIA Level 6 Initiate/Influence -- standard-setting beyond any single product's discovery process.

Defining what rigorous discovery means for the field and shaping practice externally is Dreyfus's master band and SFIA Level 7 Set strategy/Inspire -- the same register Cagan's own discovery framework occupies as an externally cited reference model.
Documenting personas and journey steps from supplied data under direction is supervised execution of a known template -- Dreyfus's novice band, SFIA Level 2 Assist.

Building usable personas and mapping journeys for one product area with normal review is Dreyfus's advanced-beginner band; it reproduces Kalbach's standard alignment-diagram structure without needing to redesign the artifact -- SFIA Level 3 Apply.

Independently modeling complex multi-actor journeys and resolving conflicting user signals is Dreyfus's competent band; Kalbach frames alignment diagrams as diagnostic tools for exactly this -- reconciling conflicting inputs into one coherent map, a judgment call with no fixed procedure.

Defining modeling standards others adopt and reconciling personas across overlapping segments is Dreyfus's proficient band, where one person's method becomes the team's codified artifact standard -- the organizational use Kalbach's own alignment-diagram practice is built for.

Setting persona and journey strategy across a portfolio and predicting shifting behavior patterns is Dreyfus's expert band and SFIA Level 6 Initiate/Influence -- reach beyond any single product's user model.

Establishing industry-recognized journey-modeling methods and teaching them widely is Dreyfus's master band and SFIA Level 7 Set strategy/Inspire -- the exact register Kalbach's own book occupies as a widely taught, externally cited method.
Gathering competitor facts and populating comparison grids under guidance is supervised execution of a defined template -- Dreyfus's novice band, SFIA Level 2 Assist.

Producing a sound competitive analysis for one product with normal review is Dreyfus's advanced-beginner band; it applies Porter's Five Forces framework as given, without adapting it to an ambiguous or unusual market structure -- SFIA Level 3 Apply.

Independently reading ambiguous markets and framing defensible positioning implications is Dreyfus's competent band; Moore's technology-adoption-lifecycle model requires exactly this judgment -- placing a market correctly relative to the chasm when the evidence is not clear-cut.

Defining the analytical approach others follow and decoding confusing competitive dynamics is Dreyfus's proficient band, where a framework is adapted and codified for a team -- extending Porter's structural analysis beyond its textbook application to a team's specific market.

Setting market-analysis strategy and anticipating structural shifts before competitors react is Dreyfus's expert band and SFIA Level 6 Initiate/Influence -- foresight beyond any single product's competitive set.

Shaping how the field interprets product-market fit and being cited externally is Dreyfus's master band and SFIA Level 7 Set strategy/Inspire -- the register both Porter's and Moore's own frameworks occupy as canonical, externally cited references.
Drafting positioning statements from a given strategy under direction is supervised execution of someone else's strategic decisions -- Dreyfus's novice band, SFIA Level 2 Assist.

Articulating strategy and positioning for one product with normal review is Dreyfus's advanced-beginner band; it fills in Dunford's positioning canvas (competitive alternatives, unique attributes, target market) as a standard template -- SFIA Level 3 Apply.

Independently setting coherent strategy amid ambiguity and defending hard trade-offs is Dreyfus's competent band; Rumelt's strategy kernel -- diagnosis, guiding policy, coherent action -- names defending real trade-offs as exactly what separates strategy from the vague goal-setting he calls bad strategy.

Defining the strategy framework teams adopt and resolving conflicting strategic bets is Dreyfus's proficient band, where Rumelt's kernel stops being one person's private discipline and becomes the team's shared framework for arbitrating competing bets.
Owning portfolio-level strategy and anticipating where the market is heading is Dreyfus's expert band and SFIA Level 6 Initiate/Influence -- strategic reach beyond any single product.

Defining what good product strategy means for the discipline and influencing practice externally is Dreyfus's master band and SFIA Level 7 Set strategy/Inspire -- the register Rumelt's and Dunford's own books occupy as externally cited definitions of good strategy and good positioning.
Maintaining roadmap items and updating status under guidance is supervised upkeep of an existing artifact -- Dreyfus's novice band, SFIA Level 2 Assist.

Building and sequencing a credible roadmap for one product with normal review is Dreyfus's advanced-beginner band; it reproduces Lombardo et al.'s theme-based roadmap format as a standard artifact -- SFIA Level 3 Apply.

Independently balancing competing priorities and replanning confidently under shifting constraints is Dreyfus's competent band; Lombardo et al. frame the roadmap as a living communication tool rather than a fixed plan, which requires exactly this judgment to re-sequence under uncertainty.

Designing the planning approach others use and resolving cross-team portfolio conflicts is Dreyfus's proficient band, where Lombardo et al.'s guidance on 'relaunching' an organization's roadmap process becomes one person's codified approach for the whole team.

Setting portfolio planning strategy and foreseeing where investment should shift next is Dreyfus's expert band and SFIA Level 6 Initiate/Influence -- reach across the whole portfolio, not one roadmap.

Defining portfolio-planning best practice for the field and being recognized for it is Dreyfus's master band and SFIA Level 7 Set strategy/Inspire -- externally referenced practice, not an internal artifact.
Translating a stated vision into concrete goals under direction is supervised decomposition of someone else's vision -- Dreyfus's novice band, SFIA Level 2 Assist.

Setting clear, measurable goals for one product area with normal review is Dreyfus's advanced-beginner band; it applies Doerr's OKR format -- an objective with two to five measurable key results -- as a standard structure, not an invented one -- SFIA Level 3 Apply.

Independently crafting a compelling vision and cascading aligned goals through ambiguity is Dreyfus's competent band; Grove's original cascading management-by-objectives model requires this judgment -- aligning goals down through an org when the path is not already mapped.

Defining goal-setting frameworks others adopt and aligning competing visions is Dreyfus's proficient band; it mirrors Doerr's own account of OKRs moving from one leader's private practice to a codified, org-wide framework other teams adopt wholesale.
Setting enduring vision across a portfolio and anticipating long-horizon shifts is Dreyfus's expert band and SFIA Level 6 Initiate/Influence -- vision reach beyond any single product's goals.

Shaping how the discipline frames product vision and being externally credible on it is Dreyfus's master band and SFIA Level 7 Set strategy/Inspire -- the register Grove's and Doerr's own frameworks occupy as originals cited industry-wide.
Writing requirements from supplied input and refining them under review is supervised drafting against someone else's problem framing -- Dreyfus's novice band, SFIA Level 2 Assist.

Authoring complete, testable specs for standard features with normal review is Dreyfus's advanced-beginner band; it applies BABOK's requirements elicitation and life-cycle-management practices as given -- SFIA Level 3 Apply.

Independently specifying ambiguous, cross-cutting features and resolving edge cases cleanly is Dreyfus's competent band; ISO/IEC/IEEE 29148's requirement-quality characteristics -- unambiguous, verifiable, necessary -- are judgment criteria applied to genuinely hard cases, not a checklist for routine ones.

Defining specification standards others adopt and untangling the hardest requirement conflicts is Dreyfus's proficient band, where BABOK's competency areas stop being individually applied and become one person's codified standard for a team.

Setting specification strategy across teams and anticipating downstream definition needs is Dreyfus's expert band and SFIA Level 6 Initiate/Influence -- reach beyond any single feature's requirements.

Defining what excellent product specification means and influencing practice externally is Dreyfus's master band and SFIA Level 7 Set strategy/Inspire -- the register a body-of-knowledge standard like ISO/IEC/IEEE 29148 itself occupies as an externally adopted reference.
Updating and grooming backlog items under direction is supervised maintenance of an existing artifact -- Dreyfus's novice band, SFIA Level 2 Assist.

Prioritizing and maintaining a healthy backlog for one team with normal review is Dreyfus's advanced-beginner band; it performs the Scrum Guide's formally defined Product Backlog refinement practice as specified -- SFIA Level 3 Apply.

Independently sequencing contested work and keeping the backlog coherent under churn is Dreyfus's competent band; Pichler's value/risk/cost prioritization techniques require exactly this judgment under contested, ambiguous conditions the Scrum Guide does not resolve.

Defining backlog practices others follow and resolving cross-team prioritization disputes is Dreyfus's proficient band, where Pichler's guidance on scaling product ownership across multiple teams becomes one person's codified standard for the group.
Setting backlog-management strategy across products and anticipating capacity tensions is Dreyfus's expert band and SFIA Level 6 Initiate/Influence -- reach beyond any single team's backlog.

Defining backlog-management best practice for the discipline and being recognized for it is Dreyfus's master band and SFIA Level 7 Set strategy/Inspire -- externally referenced practice, not one team's process.
Executing assigned launch tasks and tracking checklist items under guidance is supervised execution of someone else's launch plan -- Dreyfus's novice band, SFIA Level 2 Assist.

Coordinating a standard product launch across functions with normal review is Dreyfus's advanced-beginner band; it runs Bush's product-led launch motion as a given playbook, not an invented one -- SFIA Level 3 Apply.

Independently orchestrating complex launches and recovering when plans go sideways is Dreyfus's competent band; Moore's chasm-crossing guidance on adapting a launch when it does not land in the intended beachhead segment requires exactly this recovery judgment under ambiguity.

Defining the go-to-market playbook others adopt and rescuing high-stakes launches is Dreyfus's proficient band, where Bush's launch motion moves from one launch's execution to a codified playbook a team reuses.
Setting go-to-market strategy across the portfolio and anticipating market-timing risks is Dreyfus's expert band and SFIA Level 6 Initiate/Influence -- reach beyond any single launch.

Defining what great go-to-market means for the field and shaping external practice is Dreyfus's master band and SFIA Level 7 Set strategy/Inspire -- the register Moore's own chasm-crossing model occupies as an externally cited go-to-market reference.
Pulling and reporting defined product metrics under direction is supervised execution against someone else's metric definitions -- Dreyfus's novice band, SFIA Level 2 Assist.

Building and interpreting metric dashboards for one product with normal review is Dreyfus's advanced-beginner band; it applies Croll & Yoskovitz's One Metric That Matters framework as given -- SFIA Level 3 Apply.

Independently designing metric frameworks and drawing sound conclusions from messy data is Dreyfus's competent band; Croll & Yoskovitz's stage-based metrics model requires exactly this judgment -- selecting the right metric for an ambiguous, noisy business stage rather than a prescribed one.

Defining the measurement model teams adopt and diagnosing misleading metrics others trust is Dreyfus's proficient band, where Croll & Yoskovitz's vanity-metric diagnosis becomes one person's codified practice enforced across a team.

Setting product-analytics strategy across the org and anticipating which signals will matter is Dreyfus's expert band and SFIA Level 6 Initiate/Influence -- reach beyond any single product's dashboards.

Defining rigorous product measurement for the discipline and being cited externally on it is Dreyfus's master band and SFIA Level 7 Set strategy/Inspire -- the register Croll & Yoskovitz's own book occupies as an externally cited measurement reference.
Running predefined experiments and recording results under supervision is supervised execution of someone else's test design -- Dreyfus's novice band, SFIA Level 2 Assist.

Designing and analyzing a standard A/B test with normal review is Dreyfus's advanced-beginner band; it applies Kohavi, Tang & Xu's core randomization and overall-evaluation-criterion design as given -- SFIA Level 3 Apply.

Independently designing valid experiments and interpreting ambiguous or conflicting results is Dreyfus's competent band; Kohavi et al. document exactly this class of judgment call -- diagnosing novelty effects, sample-ratio mismatch, or Simpson's paradox in results a routine reading would miss.

Defining experimentation standards others adopt and rescuing flawed test designs is Dreyfus's proficient band, where Kohavi et al.'s guardrail-metric and trustworthiness checks become one person's codified standard a team is held to.
Setting the org's experimentation strategy and anticipating where testing should expand is Dreyfus's expert band and SFIA Level 6 Initiate/Influence -- reach beyond any single test.

Defining experimentation rigor for the discipline and influencing external practice is Dreyfus's master band and SFIA Level 7 Set strategy/Inspire -- the exact register Kohavi et al.'s book occupies as the canonical external reference on trustworthy experimentation.
Populating pricing models with supplied assumptions under direction is supervised execution against someone else's assumptions -- Dreyfus's novice band, SFIA Level 2 Assist.

Building a sound business model for one product with normal review is Dreyfus's advanced-beginner band; it fills in Osterwalder & Pigneur's Business Model Canvas as a standard template, not an invented structure -- SFIA Level 3 Apply.

Independently structuring pricing under uncertainty and defending margin trade-offs is Dreyfus's competent band; Nagle et al.'s value-based pricing approach requires exactly this judgment to defend a trade-off rather than defaulting to cost-plus math.

Defining the modeling approach others adopt and untangling complex monetization questions is Dreyfus's proficient band, where Nagle et al.'s value cascade moves from one pricing decision to a codified approach a team reuses.
Setting pricing strategy across the portfolio and anticipating market and cost shifts is Dreyfus's expert band and SFIA Level 6 Initiate/Influence -- reach beyond any single product's price.

Defining pricing and business-modeling best practice for the field and being recognized for it is Dreyfus's master band and SFIA Level 7 Set strategy/Inspire -- the register Osterwalder's and Nagle et al.'s own books occupy as canonical, externally cited references.
Preparing updates and gathering input for stakeholders under direction is supervised support of someone else's stakeholder relationship -- Dreyfus's novice band, SFIA Level 2 Assist.

Managing routine stakeholder relationships and communications with normal review is Dreyfus's advanced-beginner band; it applies Fisher & Ury's basic principled-negotiation posture -- separating people from the problem -- to low-stakes, routine interactions -- SFIA Level 3 Apply.

Independently aligning conflicting stakeholders and navigating tense executive conversations is Dreyfus's competent band; Fisher & Ury's interests-versus-positions framing requires exactly this judgment under real, high-stakes conflict rather than routine coordination.

Defining stakeholder-engagement approaches others adopt and brokering the hardest alignment is Dreyfus's proficient band; Cagan & Jones describe this as the product leader's codified practice for building executive trust that other PMs in the org are taught to follow.

Setting executive-engagement strategy and anticipating leadership concerns before they arise is Dreyfus's expert band and SFIA Level 6 Initiate/Influence -- reach beyond any single stakeholder relationship.

Defining exemplary stakeholder management for the discipline and being externally credible on it is Dreyfus's master band and SFIA Level 7 Set strategy/Inspire -- externally referenced practice, not one org's internal habit.
Logging interactions and handling routine customer requests under guidance is supervised execution of a defined support process -- Dreyfus's novice band, SFIA Level 2 Assist.

Managing standard customer and partner relationships with normal review is Dreyfus's advanced-beginner band; it runs Mehta, Steinman & Murphy's customer-success playbook on routine accounts as given -- SFIA Level 3 Apply.

Independently nurturing key accounts and resolving difficult relationship conflicts is Dreyfus's competent band; Mehta et al.'s guidance on rescuing at-risk accounts requires judgment beyond the standard playbook -- reading and repairing a relationship the playbook alone does not fix.

Defining relationship-management practices others adopt and salvaging strained partnerships is Dreyfus's proficient band, where Mehta et al.'s function-design guidance becomes one person's codified practice for how a whole team runs customer success.
Setting relationship strategy across the portfolio and anticipating partner-ecosystem shifts is Dreyfus's expert band and SFIA Level 6 Initiate/Influence -- reach beyond any single account.

Defining what excellent partner relationship management means and shaping external practice is Dreyfus's master band and SFIA Level 7 Set strategy/Inspire -- externally referenced practice, not one company's account playbook.

Placing research findings onto an existing opportunity map correctly, with coaching to distinguish opportunities from solutions, is Dreyfus's novice band and SFIA Level 2 Assist -- exactly the opportunity/solution distinction Torres names as the foundational skill a coach must first correct.

Building and maintaining the opportunity map for their area, sizing and pruning branches against evidence without prompting, is Dreyfus's advanced-beginner band; it runs Torres's opportunity-solution-tree maintenance as a standard, repeatable practice -- SFIA Level 3 Apply.

Structuring messy, contested problem spaces into maps that make trade-offs explicit, and defending why one opportunity is pursued over its siblings, is Dreyfus's competent band; this is Torres's own description of tree-pruning under ambiguity -- a judgment call, not a mechanical sizing exercise.

Reconciling overlapping opportunity maps across teams and exposing duplicate or orphaned opportunities no single team could see is Dreyfus's proficient band, where one person's mapping method is applied across multiple teams' trees -- the cross-team synthesis Torres describes as a senior discovery practice.

Making opportunity mapping an organization's default synthesis method, so investment reviews open from the mapped opportunity space, is Dreyfus's expert band and SFIA Level 6 Initiate/Influence -- the method now shapes how the org allocates investment, not just how one team plans.

Shaping how organizations represent customer opportunity at portfolio level, with methods cited and reused beyond their own organization, is Dreyfus's master band and SFIA Level 7 Set strategy/Inspire -- the exact register Torres's own opportunity-solution-tree occupies as an externally adopted method.

Writing a one-page problem statement naming the user, struggle, and evidence, with review, and separating problem from feature only when prompted, is Dreyfus's novice band and SFIA Level 2 Assist -- the basic problem/solution separation performed under coaching.

Framing work as outcomes the team can move rather than outputs to ship, and rewriting incoming feature requests into the underlying problem before triage, is Dreyfus's advanced-beginner band; it applies Seiden's outcome-versus-output distinction as a standard reframing habit -- SFIA Level 3 Apply.

Setting the outcome a product is accountable for and publicly re-framing efforts that drift into output-counting is Dreyfus's competent band; Seiden frames holding a team to an outcome under drift and ambiguity as the harder, judgment-driven half of outcome-based work.

Arbitrating problem framing across teams and re-cutting problem boundaries drawn along org lines instead of customer lines is Dreyfus's proficient band, where Seiden's outcome-based team design -- organizing around outcomes, not org charts -- becomes a codified practice applied across multiple teams.

Defining an organization's outcome architecture -- how team-level outcomes ladder to organizational results -- and retiring vanity outcomes is Dreyfus's expert band and SFIA Level 6 Initiate/Influence -- architecture spanning the whole org's outcome structure, not one team's.

Framing an organization's hardest, ownerless problems into tractable outcome statements executives fund is Dreyfus's master band and SFIA Level 7 Set strategy/Inspire -- the register Seiden's own book occupies as an externally cited outcome-framing doctrine.

Restating a feature request as the job the customer is hiring it for -- circumstance and progress sought -- with coaching is Dreyfus's novice band and SFIA Level 2 Assist -- applying Christensen et al.'s core JTBD vocabulary under supervision before it becomes an independent lens.

Mapping the main jobs in their area from interview evidence, and identifying what customers currently hire and where those hires fail, is Dreyfus's advanced-beginner band; it applies Christensen et al.'s hiring/firing metaphor independently but to standard, well-bounded cases -- SFIA Level 3 Apply.

Anchoring a product's definition and boundaries in its core job, and using it to identify non-obvious competitors, is Dreyfus's competent band; this is Christensen et al.'s own milkshake-study move -- spotting a job's true competing alternatives when they are not obviously products at all.

Aligning job maps across teams into one view of customer progress, exposing where customers must stitch products together to finish one job, is Dreyfus's proficient band, where a single-product JTBD lens becomes a codified, portfolio-spanning map others build on.

Using jobs analysis to shape organization-level portfolio choices -- which jobs are served end-to-end, which are exited -- is Dreyfus's expert band and SFIA Level 6 Initiate/Influence -- portfolio reach beyond any single product's job.

Framing markets and strategy in jobs terms that reveal disruption threats early, with analyses that influence practice beyond their organization, is Dreyfus's master band and SFIA Level 7 Set strategy/Inspire -- the register Christensen's own disruption and jobs theory occupies as an externally cited doctrine.

Listing assumptions behind a proposed feature, sorting them by risk with coaching, and running a prescribed simple test is Dreyfus's novice band and SFIA Level 2 Assist -- a supervised first pass through Ries's build-measure-learn loop.

Identifying the riskiest assumption before build and matching the test type to it -- prototype, painted door, concierge -- with pass/fail defined in advance is Dreyfus's advanced-beginner band; it applies Bland & Osterwalder's experiment library as a standard lookup, matching test type to assumption -- SFIA Level 3 Apply.

Surfacing assumptions others treat as facts and designing test sequences that retire the most risk per unit effort is Dreyfus's competent band; this is Bland & Osterwalder's assumptions mapping -- ranking by importance times evidence -- applied with judgment to sequence tests for maximum risk retirement, not a fixed checklist.

Standardizing how multiple teams express and rank risk, and rejecting validation theater -- tests that can only confirm, never falsify -- is Dreyfus's proficient band, where Bland & Osterwalder's explicit warning against non-falsifiable tests becomes one person's codified standard enforced across teams.

Building discovery-testing capability into an organization's investment process, so funding follows tested assumptions and a first test costs hours, is Dreyfus's expert band and SFIA Level 6 Initiate/Influence -- capability built into the org's process, not one team's habit.

Structuring bets too big to A/B as staged, falsifiable commitments, with a validation doctrine cited and adopted beyond their organization, is Dreyfus's master band and SFIA Level 7 Set strategy/Inspire -- the register Ries's original validated-learning doctrine occupies as an externally cited reference.

Learning the domain deliberately -- shadowing customers, reading industry sources, asking how the system actually works -- and using domain vocabulary correctly is Dreyfus's novice band and SFIA Level 2 Assist -- the supervised, deliberate acquisition phase before independent fluency.

Answering most domain questions without deferring and correcting domain errors in specs and designs is Dreyfus's advanced-beginner band; it applies Cagan's framing of market/domain knowledge as a core, day-to-day PM competency without yet catching risks others miss -- SFIA Level 3 Apply.

Being the recognized domain reference for a product, whom others check facts with, and spotting domain-driven risks others miss is Dreyfus's competent band; this is Cagan's value risk in practice -- domain judgment about what will actually work for the customer that a less fluent PM cannot supply.

Connecting domain knowledge across teams and catching where one roadmap violates another domain's constraints is Dreyfus's proficient band, where individual domain expertise scales into cross-team risk-catching -- Cagan's discussion of domain fluency extending beyond a single product's boundary.

Representing an organization's domain understanding externally -- industry forums, advisory boards, analyst briefings -- is Dreyfus's expert band and SFIA Level 6 Initiate/Influence -- external representation on the org's behalf, not internal reference status alone.

Anticipating domain evolution and positioning portfolios for it before consensus forms is Dreyfus's master band and SFIA Level 7 Set strategy/Inspire -- foresight that shapes the discipline's direction, not just fluency with its current state.
Maintaining the inventory and prepping governance materials under direction is Dreyfus's novice band -- explicit rules, no independent judgment on governance calls yet.
Running intake and scoring independently inside a fixed framework is Dreyfus's advanced-beginner band and SFIA Level 3 Apply -- situational judgment stays inside guardrails set by others.

Facilitating contentious prioritization and setting local governance rules autonomously is the Dreyfus competent band; PMI's Standard for Portfolio Management treats governance-model choice as a portfolio-manager judgment call, not a scripted intake step.

Defining the prioritization/governance model other portfolio owners adopt is SFIA Level 5 Ensure-and-advise -- the practitioner now authors the framework PMI's standard describes rather than applying someone else's.

Setting enterprise portfolio-governance strategy and anticipating investment shifts matches SFIA Level 6 Initiate-and-influence -- governance choices now shape strategy across the whole investment portfolio, the top scope band PMI's standard describes.

Defining best-practice portfolio governance for the discipline and being externally recognized is SFIA Level 7 Set-strategy-and-inspire -- the practitioner now operates at the level that writes standards like PMI's rather than following them.
Recording benefit measures and tracking against plan under guidance is the Dreyfus novice band: applying a prescribed tracking template, no interpretation of ambiguous value claims yet.

Independently monitoring benefits and flagging routine shortfalls under review is Dreyfus's advanced-beginner band / SFIA Level 3 Apply -- recognizing common shortfall patterns without owning the value case.

Defining value cases for ambiguous initiatives and owning realization end-to-end is the Dreyfus competent band; PMI's Benefits Realization Management guide places case-authorship and life-cycle ownership at the practitioner-autonomy tier, not the reporting-only tier.

Defining the benefits-realization methodology other teams adopt, and salvaging value others miss, is SFIA Level 5 Ensure-and-advise -- the practitioner now authors the life-cycle model PMI's guide describes rather than executing someone else's.

Setting enterprise value-tracking strategy and anticipating how benefits should be measured next is SFIA Level 6 Initiate-and-influence -- scope moves from a single value case to how the whole enterprise measures value.

Defining leading benefits-realization practice for the field and being sought externally is SFIA Level 7 Set-strategy-and-inspire -- this is the authorship tier that produces guidance like PMI's, not the tier that consumes it.
Compiling status data into standard reports under supervision is the Dreyfus novice band -- following a fixed reporting template with no interpretive judgment.
Independently producing routine dashboards and summaries with review is Dreyfus's advanced-beginner band / SFIA Level 3 Apply -- the format is given, the analyst fills it in.
